## Where we are

::: {.incremental}
- All earlier workshops quietly **dropped rows with missing values**
- Today: **why that can mislead**, and how to **describe** missing data
- By the end you can:
  - describe the **amount and pattern** of missingness
  - name the three **mechanisms** (MCAR, MAR, MNAR)
  - **explore** whether missingness depends on observed data
  - say what the data **cannot** tell you
:::

## Our data: an NCD cohort with gaps

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **2,000 adults** (synthetic): age, sex, education, BMI, smoking, activity, SBP, HbA1c
- Missing: **BMI 26%**, **HbA1c 21%**, **activity 12%**, **smoking 9%**, **SBP 6%**
- Age, sex and education are complete
- Only **45%** of adults have **every** variable
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
ncd |> head(8)
```
:::
:::

# Topic 1 — Mechanisms {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Three mechanisms

| Mechanism | Missingness depends on... | Example here |
|---|---|---|
| **MCAR** (completely at random) | nothing | a form lost at random (smoking, 9%) |
| **MAR** (at random) | **observed** data | BMI missing more in **older men with a high SBP** |
| **MNAR** (not at random) | the **missing value itself** | high **HbA1c** more often missing |

::: {.key}
The names are confusing: in **MAR** the missingness is **not random** at all; it is **explained by other observed variables**. That is what allows us to **correct** for it.
:::

## Why it matters

::: {.incremental}
- **MCAR**: complete-case analysis is **unbiased** but loses **precision**
- **MAR**: complete-case can be **biased**; **multiple imputation** (and likelihood methods) are **valid**
- **MNAR**: **no method** is valid without an **assumption** about the missing values: do a **sensitivity analysis**
- You **cannot tell MAR from MNAR** from the observed data alone
:::

# Topic 2 — Describing missing data {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## How much and which pattern?

```{r}
round(100 * colMeans(is.na(ncd)), 1)
sum(complete.cases(ncd))
```

```{r}
md.pattern(dat, plot = FALSE) |> head(3)
```

::: {.key}
**905** adults (45%) are complete; then **BMI alone missing (296)** and **HbA1c alone (196)**: **26 patterns** in all.
:::

## A picture

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-height: 4.4
gg_miss_upset(dat, nsets = 5)
```

::: {.key}
An **UpSet plot** shows the commonest **combinations** of missing variables. Also useful: `vis_miss(dat)` and `miss_var_summary(dat)`.
:::

# Topic 3 — What drives the missingness? {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Compare with and without BMI

```{r}
dat |> group_by(bmi_missing = is.na(bmi)) |> summarise(n = n(), age = round(mean(age), 1), sbp = round(mean(sbp, na.rm = TRUE)), men = round(mean(sex == "Male"), 2))
```

::: {.warn}
Adults with a missing BMI are **older (54 vs 45)**, **more often men (63% vs 44%)** and have a **higher SBP (135 vs 121)**. The data are **not MCAR**. Because the differences are in **observed** variables, **MAR** is plausible.
:::

## Model the missingness

```{r}
m_miss <- glm(is.na(bmi) ~ age + sex + education + sbp, data = dat, family = binomial)
round(summary(m_miss)$coefficients, 3)
```

::: {.incremental}
- Age, male sex and **especially SBP** (z = 16) predict a missing BMI; education does not
- This is evidence for **MAR**: and a warning that **SBP, the outcome, must be in the imputation model**
:::

## Little's MCAR test

```{r}
dat |> mutate(male = as.integer(sex == "Male")) |> select(age, male, bmi, smoker, activity, sbp, hba1c) |> mcar_test()
```

::: {.warn}
p < 0.001: **MCAR is rejected**. That does **not** prove **MAR**: **MNAR cannot be tested** from the data, because the values that decide it are the ones **you do not have**. Argue it from **subject knowledge** (why would a value be missing?), then do a **sensitivity analysis** (Session 5).
:::

## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("m1q1", "Older men are more often missing BMI, and they also have a higher observed SBP. Which mechanism is the most plausible?",
         c("Missing at random: missingness depends on observed variables",
           "Missing completely at random: missingness is unrelated to the data",
           "Missing not at random: missingness depends on the unobserved BMI itself",
           "No mechanism applies, since a part of the BMI values is observed"), answer = 1,
         explain = "Missingness that is explained by observed age, sex and SBP is the definition of MAR. MNAR cannot be ruled out from the data, but MAR is the working assumption here.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("m1q2", "Little's test rejects MCAR (p < 0.001). What can you conclude?",
         c("The data are MNAR, so multiple imputation cannot be used on them",
           "The data are not MCAR, but this does not tell MAR from MNAR",
           "The data are MAR, since MCAR is the other simple mechanism left",
           "Nothing can be concluded, because the test applies to categorical variables"), answer = 2,
         explain = "Rejecting MCAR shows that missingness depends on something. Whether that is observed (MAR) or unobserved (MNAR) cannot be learned from the test.")
```

## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("m1q3", "Why can MNAR not be tested using the observed data?",
         c("The sample is too small for a test to be able to detect the effect",
           "Tests exist for it, but they need survey weights in order to work",
           "MNAR occurs when a large share of the values (above half) is missing",
           "The values that determine the missingness are not observed"), answer = 4,
         explain = "MNAR means missingness depends on the missing value itself. Without those values there is nothing to compare, so the assumption rests on subject knowledge and sensitivity analysis.")
```

## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("m1q4", "Only 45% of adults are complete. What is the main problem with complete-case analysis here?",
         c("It loses precision, and may be biased if complete cases are selected",
           "It makes the standard errors too small, because fewer adults are analysed in the model",
           "It turns the variables into categories, which loses information on each variable",
           "It cannot be run in R unless the missing values are first recoded as zero"), answer = 1,
         explain = "More than half of the sample is discarded, and if missingness depends on the variables in the analysis, the remaining adults are a selected group.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("m1q5", "A pattern table shows 905 complete rows and 296 rows with only BMI missing. What does it help you decide?",
         c("Whether the missing values in this dataset are random or not random in nature",
           "Which adults should be deleted from the dataset before the analysis starts",
           "Which variables are missing together, and where imputation matters most",
           "How many imputations are needed to get unbiased estimates from the data"), answer = 3,
         explain = "A pattern table describes the amount and combinations of missingness. It does not identify the mechanism or the number of imputations.")
```

## Score and take-home

**Your score: <span class="quiz-score"></span>**

::: {.incremental}
- **MCAR / MAR / MNAR**: what the missingness depends on
- **Describe**: % missing, complete cases, patterns, plots
- **Compare** observed variables between complete and incomplete; model the missingness
- **MNAR cannot be tested**: argue it, then do a sensitivity analysis
- Include the **outcome** among the variables that explain missingness
:::
